prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identity of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: The first round did not weaken the case for B035 and it clarified what the disagreement is. All six of us describe the same chain: proglucagon processing, the truncated active peptide, its glucose-dependent insulinotropic and appetite-related actions, receptor biology, and then long-acting agonists confirmed by independent outcome trials in glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal disease. That is a discernible change in a field, it is mature, and none of us raised a maturity objection. The remaining question is what the prize is for. I still read it as a prize for the discovery of how the incretin system works and which peptide form is active, with the therapy as the demonstration that the discovery was correct and consequential. On that reading Holst (human physiology and secretion), Drucker (receptor biology and the proglucagon-peptide axis) and Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active form) are the discovery-side trio. A single-part prize is the right size for it. A second part could be added only by cutting one of these three, and that would damage an achievement we all rank first.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still attribution, and round 1 did not remove it. Four credited names need three seats, so any trio leaves out either Knudsen, whose long-acting analogues turned the hormone into a drug, or a name tied to the discovery side. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) form is publicly contested, and I cannot settle it from the files. Five of us, including me, are naming her partly from recollection of the literature, which is a weak basis for a seat. Habener-type contributions are outside the credited names, so even my preferred trio can be called incomplete. A physiology-led citation also risks reading as a prize for the idea and not the medicine, and the success of the drug class is commercial as well as scientific. I accept all of these costs. I judge them lower than the cost of either leaving the discovery of the active peptide unattributed or splitting the credit across a two-part prize.

responses.point: She keeps Drucker, Holst and Knudsen so the prize spans physiology to therapy, and she will not rest a seat on a priority question that, by our own admission, is unverified recollection. She says she would revisit if the Mojsov record can be established cleanly.
responses.response: Her objection is the one I find hardest to answer, because it turns my own caveat against me. I cannot verify the priority record, and I agree that an unverified claim is a poor basis for a seat. I still do not move, for two reasons. First, the contest over Mojsov concerns who was first and how credit is shared, but not whether the identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide was a real discovery step on which the later pharmacology depends. That step is what the citation names. Second, with Knudsen in place of Mojsov the citation has to cover the whole path from physiology to analogue design, which makes it a development prize and spreads it over a team whose credit is shared inside a company. I do not call her trio unreasonable, and as I said in round 1 I would not oppose it if the committee decides the prize should honour translation. What I ask is that the committee decide that question openly, as a choice between a discovery citation and a development citation, and not let it be settled by whichever name feels safer. If the committee cannot agree on the Mojsov record, her configuration is the better fallback than a trio with a hole in it.

responses.point: He keeps Mojsov on the discovery-side trio but says he could support Knudsen if the citation states plainly that it recognises the drug-design contribution, and he sees the unfolded protein response (B047) as a good candidate whose clinical consequence is still indirect.
responses.response: I agree with his conditional position, and it answers the chair's question about wording. A citation can be fair to either trio only if it says what it honours. Mine names the physiology and the identity of the active form. His version for a Knudsen trio would have to name drug design explicitly, and I think that would make it a different achievement and not a variant of the same one. On B047 I remain where I was. Walter and Mori are a clean pair with decades of independent confirmation, and I ranked it fifth. But it does not yet show the effect on medicine that B035 shows, and it has no urgency that outweighs the GLP-1 case. I would not use it as a second part, because that forces the same cut of an incretin laureate. I would keep it for a later year.

responses.point: He prefers a prize built on the discovery of the hormone and its active form and warns that a two-part split would force a reduction of the incretin credit, making the harder attribution problem worse. He says he would move toward Knudsen if the evidence on Mojsov proved weak.
responses.response: I agree with his main structural point and I have changed my own view in one respect because of it. In round 1 I treated B011 and B014 as possible second parts for a later round. After reading the exchange I no longer think a second part is feasible this year, because the three-person cap means it could only be bought by removing Drucker, Holst or Mojsov, and nobody has argued that any of them should go. On Mojsov versus Knudsen we differ only in the threshold. He would move to Knudsen if the priority evidence were weak, and I would hold Mojsov unless the evidence shows that the identification of the active form is not hers to share. We should be honest that neither of us can test that from the files, so the disagreement is about how to act under uncertainty. I prefer to keep the name tied to the discovery step that the citation describes. I also take his point about the commercial character of the success. It is a reason to keep the citation on physiology, where the scientific judgement is ours to make.

responses.point: He accepts that Mojsov's priority cannot be settled from the record, but holds the discovery-weighted trio because the neuroendocrine appetite actions depend on the biology that Drucker and Holst described. He would not make B028 a second part, since it dilutes a unanimous first choice.
responses.response: I agree on both points, and his argument about appetite physiology strengthens the discovery-side reading. The actions that explain the weight effect belong to the biology of the peptide, not to the engineering of the analogue. I also agree that B028 is clean and mature, and I ranked it last of my eight only because it is a different kind of achievement, and not because I doubt it. Where I differ slightly is on how much weight Habener-type contributions should carry. He treats them mainly as a caveat on the citation. I think they limit how strongly the citation can claim to cover the whole discovery. For that reason I would keep the wording to the physiology of GLP-1 and the identity of its active form, and avoid language such as 'the discovery of GLP-1' that would claim more than a three-name trio can fairly carry.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) form supports a seat. I cannot check this from the files, and my account rests on recollection, as do several colleagues' accounts.
Whether the committee wants a discovery citation or one that also names drug development. This choice decides between a Mojsov trio and a Knudsen trio more than any new evidence is likely to.
How far the absence of Habener-type contributions from the credited names should count against any B035 trio.

Whether B011 or B014 would be a clean second part in a later year, given the upstream credit problems for each (Philadelphia chromosome and ABL work and the role of Novartis for B011, Eshhar for B014).
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted ballots and I see no need for recusal. My documented ties are to Ronald Evans (nuclear receptor work at the Salk Institute), Johan Ericson (collaboration at Karolinska Institutet) and, by co-authorship, Per Svenningsson and Abdel El Manira. None of these people is a credited name on any shortlisted ballot. I note them for transparency. No new tie was introduced by the round-1 exchange, and the ties that other members disclosed (El-Manira with me, Svenningsson with me) concern dopamine-neuron and stem-cell work unrelated to any shortlisted ballot.
